name: DemandSense
about: The LinkedIn Ads analytics company behind the Standard. Writes the base rules every skill checks against, tests each contribution on real accounts before it is published, and keeps the library free

title: Read frequency and penetration together
why: One number alone doesn't tell you what to fix.

advises.text: Campaign Manager reports reach, average frequency and audience penetration for each campaign.

page.adds: Read penetration and accounts reached first, then frequency, then CTR, and decide from the combination. Read them at 30, 60 and 90 days.
page.reason: An average frequency of 3 can mean part of the list saw the ad a dozen times while most of it saw nothing. Once penetration stops growing, more budget only raises frequency on the people already reached.
page.mattersLess: Average frequency on its own is enough when the audience is small and penetration is high, because most people are close to the average.

signs.see: Frequency under target, penetration healthy
signs.do: Add budget, or narrow the audience so the same budget repeats more.

signs.see: Penetration stalls around 50% with frequency on target
signs.do: That's a reachability ceiling. Export the accounts with no impressions and reach them through other channels, like Meta, programmatic or outbound.

signs.see: Frequency above target, CTR falling
signs.do: Rotate the weakest ads before you touch budget (rule 03).

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Read them together, and over 90 days, not one week. On a signal list low reach is still the usual problem, so I check how much of the list has seen me at all before I touch the average.”

title: Set separate frequency targets for cold and warm audiences
why: Cold audiences run low and wide. Warm audiences need repetition.

advises.text: Campaign Manager reports average frequency for each campaign. Frequency targets are left to the advertiser.

page.adds: Cold: low and wide, reach first. Warm in-feed: around 15 to 25 impressions per person over 90 days (our current working range).
page.reason: Cold advertising is there to reach people and fill the warm audiences, so repetition is mostly wasted on it. Warm audiences already know you, and that's where repetition turns into trust and action.
page.mattersLess: One target for the whole account is fine while it runs a single audience layer, such as a new account that only runs cold campaigns.

signs.see: One frequency target for the whole account
signs.do: Set one for cold and a higher one for warm.

signs.see: Cold frequency rising while penetration stays flat
signs.do: Widen reach before you add repetition.

signs.see: Warm audiences under 15 impressions a person in 90 days
signs.do: Move budget into the warm layer until it reaches its range.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Two targets, yes. But to me, a company with a fresh, dated signal is warm whether it clicked or not, and a company that only fits stays cold. Run a signal company in the cold band, under 3 to 5 views in 90 days, and it barely sees you right when it has a reason to buy. So I plan about 5 a month.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “I aim for a frequency of 3–5 for cold audiences and 10–15 for warm, and try not to go over 15.”

title: Call it fatigue only when frequency is high and CTR keeps falling
why: Either signal on its own isn't fatigue.

advises.text: LinkedIn recommends several ads per ad set and shifts delivery toward the ads it predicts will perform best.

page.adds: Rotate the losers, never the proven winners. A winner keeps running until the data says it's tired.
page.reason: An ad that has run for a while has collected likes, comments and shares, and that social proof lowers its cost per click. Refreshing everything on a calendar throws that away along with the ads that were actually tired.
page.mattersLess: Letting LinkedIn favour the strongest ads is the right default. It already moves delivery away from the weak ones, so most weeks there is nothing to change by hand.

signs.see: Frequency high, CTR holding
signs.do: Leave it. Winners keep the social proof they've built.

signs.see: CTR down for one week
signs.do: Check again next week.

signs.see: Frequency above target, CTR down two to three weeks running
signs.do: Replace the weakest ads. Keep the winners.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “Falling CTR is the best indicator of fatigue in my mind. The frequency number is so opaque (you can't actually tell how often the most active audience members are being reached) that I use it as a precursor clue to what's happening, and then confirm with falling CTR. Sometimes CTR starts to fall even when frequency looks OK.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “Correct. I look for a trend of CTR dropping over several weeks.”

title: Judge Text, Spotlight and Follower ads on reach and CPM, not CTR
why: These formats are there for efficient visibility, so clicks are the wrong measure.

advises.text: Campaign Manager reports every format on the same metrics, so you choose which one fits each format's job.

page.adds: Single image and video carry the message and the ask. Text, Spotlight and Follower ads give low-cost presence under warm audiences, on a 180-day window. They also work as low-cost broad reach.
page.reason: Coverage formats cost a fraction of in-feed per thousand impressions. Judged on CTR they always lose, which is why many accounts switch off the cheapest way to stay visible across a long sales cycle. They're desktop-only and run alongside in-feed, never in place of it.
page.mattersLess: CTR is the right measure for in-feed formats whose job is the click: single image, video, document and carousel ads.

signs.see: Text ads with a tiny CTR and a high cost per click
signs.do: Judge them on CPM, impressions and accounts reached.

signs.see: Coverage ads switched off over cost per lead
signs.do: Turn them back on under warm audiences, or as low-cost broad reach, and measure them on reach.

signs.see: Coverage ads running on 90-day audiences
signs.do: Move them to 180-day audiences.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “Very much agree with this. Also judge them by CPC, since they're so cheap. And judge Follower ads by cost per follow if company follows are actually the goal of the ad set.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “I use them less and less. They skew the total performance numbers (they lower CPM) but have minimal impact on overall campaign performance.”

title: Split campaigns only when one segment clearly outperforms the rest
why: A segment earns its own campaign by performing two to three times better or worse than the rest.

advises.text: Campaign Manager has built-in A/B tests for comparing audiences, creative and placements.

page.adds: Retargeting and cold both start broad. A split comes when a gap shows up in the data, not up front.
page.reason: Every split divides the budget and the creative work. Splitting early gives each campaign too little spend to learn from, so the segments that deserve their own budget never show themselves.
page.mattersLess: Once a segment stands out, a LinkedIn A/B test is the clean way to confirm it before you split the budget for good.

signs.see: One industry or size band is two to three times more efficient
signs.do: Give it its own campaign, budget and message.

signs.see: Many small campaigns, none with much budget
signs.do: Merge them. Split again when a segment stands out.

signs.see: The biggest companies on a list take most of the impressions
signs.do: Split the list into company-size bands with their own budgets.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “I'd add a floor before any split. Each part's ad set has to clear 300 member accounts, and its budget still has to pay for about 5 views a person a month. If it can't, keep it in one ad set.”

title: Watch for budget drifting to junior roles
why: Junior roles click more and cost less, so a campaign with mixed seniorities slowly shifts its budget to them.

advises.text: Seniority is a targeting option, and delivery is optimized toward the result you choose, such as clicks or leads.

page.adds: When delivery shows the drift, decision-makers get their own campaign and budget, so cheaper clicks can't take it.
page.reason: Junior researchers often click two to three times more than VPs, while VPs cost more per impression. Optimizing for the cheapest result follows whoever acts most, so a mixed audience drifts junior unless you split it.
page.mattersLess: One blended campaign is fine when every seniority in it can buy, or while the budget is too small to split (rule 05).

signs.see: Junior seniorities take a large share of impressions
signs.do: Put decision-makers in their own campaign, with their own budget and bid.

signs.see: Cost per lead falling while the junior share rises
signs.do: Check lead quality by seniority before calling it a win.

signs.see: Lead quality varies by seniority, all in one campaign
signs.do: Split senior titles out so their budget is set on purpose.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “Where this is an issue, I like to break seniorities up into separate ad sets. LinkedIn can't cheat you by giving you too many junior folks in an ad set that's set up only for junior roles.”

voices.name: Joshua Stout
voices.quote: “Often it's not really a junior position but a practitioner or end-user role. For example, Data Architect and Data Scientist count as Entry in job seniority. ... I tend to segment by practitioners, their leaders (management or upper-level leadership), and then executives.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “Seniority isn't a reliable indicator. A specialist can sometimes be quite a senior decision-maker but still be tagged as a specialist. I rely more on specific job titles than on seniority.”

title: To exclude SDRs, exclude Sales, not Business Development
why: Excluding Business Development to remove SDRs removes the decision-makers too.

advises.text: Job function is a standard targeting option, and any function can be excluded.

page.adds: In our experience, founders, owners, CEOs and presidents of smaller companies sit under Business Development, while SDRs and BDRs sit under Sales. To exclude sales-floor roles, exclude Sales or junior seniorities, never Business Development.
page.reason: At smaller companies, founders, owners and CEOs often sit under Business Development in LinkedIn's job-function data, while SDRs and BDRs sit under Sales. Exclude Business Development to lose the SDRs and you lose the buyer at exactly the companies where the founder signs.
page.mattersLess: Excluding Business Development can be right when your buyers work at large companies, where BD teams aren't part of the deal.

signs.see: Business Development excluded to keep SDRs out
signs.do: Exclude Sales, or junior seniorities in Sales, instead.

signs.see: Founder-led companies targeted by job title
signs.do: Target the function with senior seniorities instead.

signs.see: You sell to sales leaders
signs.do: Exclude junior seniorities in Sales, not the whole function, or you remove the buyer.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “This is super important, and LinkedIn doesn't make it clear, so most advertisers get it wrong. If I want to reach CEOs, presidents and owners, I'll use the Business Development job function with CXO seniority. If I want to reach business development folks, I'll use the Business Development function with the lower seniorities. I don't often exclude SDRs specifically, but I like the idea of excluding the Sales function, or even business development titles.”

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Put job titles in an ad set and Campaign Manager won't let you exclude seniorities or functions at all. I hit ‘Job Seniorities may not be excluded when Job Titles is included.’ on my own account in September. So it's titles or those exclusions. You don't get both.”

title: Check every month who your ads actually reach
why: Campaign totals don't show who the budget actually reached. LinkedIn's demographics report does.

advises.text: The demographics report in Campaign Manager breaks delivery down by seniority, job function, company size and more.

page.adds: Once a month, check the demographics report by seniority, function and company size, and read the last ten profiles that engaged or became leads.
page.reason: Targeting choices interact. An expansion setting, an overlapping attribute or a missed exclusion can widen delivery without anyone noticing, and a monthly look at the report plus ten real profiles catches it early.
page.mattersLess: If the report matches your targeting month after month, a quick look is enough.

signs.see: Company sizes or seniorities you didn't plan for
signs.do: Fix the setting that widened delivery, then read ten engaged profiles.

signs.see: A function or seniority you never targeted shows up
signs.do: Check Audience Expansion is set the way you meant, then exclude it.

signs.see: Totals look fine, so nobody checks
signs.do: Open the demographics report once a month.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Open it by company too, not just by seniority and size. From 7 Aug to 5 Sep 2026, one of my ad sets got 49% of its clicks (350 of 708) from people listed at ‘Stealth AI Startup’, a placeholder page people pick instead of a real employer. Strike those out by exact name before you read any CTR.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “I check demographics weekly. Monthly is too slow to adjust.”

title: Count an audience as warm only once it's big enough to serve ads
why: Traffic and followers only count once they're in a matched audience big enough to run.

advises.text: Matched audiences only collect people from the day they're created, and need 300 members before they serve.

page.adds: Warm-first only applies to audiences that can serve today. A new account behaves like a cold one for its first weeks, even with real traffic. Create every audience on day one, and plan from the matched count, not the rows uploaded.
page.reason: Plenty of plans stall because they assumed warm audiences that existed in principle but not in the ad account. Checking what can actually serve fixes the pacing before any money goes in.
page.mattersLess: Starting with retargeting is right when the account already has matched audiences that can serve, or a CRM list to upload.

signs.see: A new account with no tag history plans to start with retargeting
signs.do: Start cold to build the audience. Add retargeting once it can serve.

signs.see: A retargeting audience under about 1,000 members
signs.do: Keep feeding it before you spend on it.

signs.see: A CRM or email list ready to upload
signs.do: Upload it on day one. It's warm right away. Plan from the matched count.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “I don't mind creating an ad set while the audience is still too small, because I know that as soon as it hits 300, LinkedIn can start serving impressions right away. Since it wasn't large enough to run before, there's no danger to reported traffic, followers or spend, because there wouldn't be any.”

voices.name: Joshua Stout
voices.quote: “I've always believed you start retargeting as soon as the audience is usable at 300. I want my ads in front of a prospect as early as possible. You can always start at $10 a day and increase the budget as the audience grows.”

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “A CRM or email contact has had a touchpoint with you, so it's not fully cold. But a dated signal beats familiarity. A company that just hired a new VP is warmer than someone you emailed a year ago. So I rank a fresh signal first and the familiar contact second.”

title: Spend on warm audiences before cold ones
why: A colder audience earns budget once the warmer ones reach their frequency range.

advises.text: Budget is set per campaign, so the order you fund audiences in is up to you.

page.adds: Order: your own data first (CRM, past leads, site visitors, engaged accounts), then in-market search, then account lists built from signals, then broad targeting.
page.reason: Unused first-party data is the cheapest audience you'll ever have. Spreading a small budget across many cold campaigns gives each one too little to show anything. Cold still runs from month one in most accounts, because it builds the audience everything else draws from.
page.mattersLess: Funding cold first is right on a new account, before any warm audience can serve (rule 09).

signs.see: Most budget on cold while warm sits underused
signs.do: Fund warm up to its frequency target first.

signs.see: More campaigns than the budget can support
signs.do: Run fewer. About $20 a day per campaign is the floor for one to learn.

signs.see: Warm audiences at their frequency range
signs.do: Open the next colder audience, in order.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Agree, fill warm first. When warm is full I add a second signal list from the same market, and the cold fit-only list carries whatever's left. I never widen a signal list just for size.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “I'd tend to disagree, as I get most of my results from cold audiences. Warm audiences get saturated very quickly for most clients, so the opportunity is in cold. I rarely spend more than 20–25% on retargeting and warm audiences.”

title: Start Lead Gen Forms early, then narrow them to recent engagers
why: Open the conversion layer as soon as a warm audience can serve, then tighten it to recent engagers.

advises.text: Lead Gen Forms pre-fill members' profile details, which makes them the easiest way to convert on LinkedIn.

page.adds: Start the form on the 90-day audience. Once the 30-day audience can serve, the form moves there and the 90-day audience gets nurture and trust content.
page.reason: Opening the conversion layer early starts offer testing sooner. Narrowing it later keeps the ask on people whose interest is recent.
page.mattersLess: A form to a cold audience can work for a light offer people want straight away, like a report or a checklist.

signs.see: Demo or sales-call offers running to cold audiences
signs.do: Move the demo to warm. Give cold something lighter.

signs.see: Forms held back for a calendar date
signs.do: Launch on the first warm audience that can serve: day one with a CRM list, usually weeks 4 to 8 on a cold start. Sync the form to the CRM the day it launches.

signs.see: One form running to the whole warm audience
signs.do: Start on the 90-day audience, then move it to 30-day engagers once that can serve.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “So good! Especially with small budgets, I usually start with any retargeting audiences I can get my hands on, since we really need a large enough audience. But once that audience has grown and is actively serving, we know that someone who interacted with our ads yesterday is more likely to re-engage than someone who interacted 350 days ago. It's hard to remember to actually do, but it's such good practice to go back in and tighten the time window, so retargeting audiences hold only the most recent engagers, the people who can be expected to remember interacting with the brand.”

title: Report exposure, influence and attribution separately
why: Exposed, influenced and attributed are three different claims.

advises.text: Conversion tracking credits conversions inside the click and view windows you set. LinkedIn also offers revenue attribution reporting for CRM-connected accounts.

page.adds: Use the lowest word the evidence supports. Leave out renewals and existing customers before claiming influence on new business. Report the three as separate numbers, never added together.
page.reason: B2B deals take longer than any click window, so last touch undercounts LinkedIn. Overclaiming wins one meeting and loses the next. A smaller number you can defend lasts longer.
page.mattersLess: Conversion windows are the right tool for comparing campaigns with each other, and for short cycles where the deal closes inside the window.

signs.see: An account saw your ads
signs.do: Report it as exposed.

signs.see: Months of impressions before the deal was created
signs.do: Report it as influenced, with the dates beside the deal date. Leave renewals and existing customers out.

signs.see: A tracked click or conversion ties LinkedIn to the deal
signs.do: Report it as attributed, on its own line.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “If you want to say caused, hold out about 100 companies with a signal that get no ads and no messages all quarter. Report meetings as two counts with both group sizes, never a percentage, because a percentage on half a meeting means nothing.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “Yes, but in practice every client has their own take on what counts as influenced.”

title: Give sales a weekly ranked list of warm accounts, checked against the CRM
why: Hot accounts, ranked, with who engaged and where they sit in the CRM. Never a raw visitor feed.

advises.text: The Company Engagement Report in Campaign Manager shows which companies are engaging with your ads, and how much.

page.adds: Filter to ICP fit, then rank by how many people and roles engaged over time. Check the CRM before sales touches anything. Open deals go to their owner, customers to their account manager, new accounts to SDRs.
page.reason: Outreach on a single signal reaches good accounts at the wrong moment, and an SDR pitching an account that's mid-deal embarrasses everyone. Context turns a signal into a reason to reach out.
page.mattersLess: For a short account list with one owner, the Company Engagement Report can be enough on its own to brief sales.

signs.see: One visit, or one intent spike
signs.do: Watch list, until more signals follow.

signs.see: Two or more people in different roles at one account, back for pricing or case studies
signs.do: Top of this week's list, with who engaged and what they read.

signs.see: A warm account with an open deal
signs.do: Send it to the deal owner. Keep SDRs off it.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Count companies on your list, not clicks or people. My default line is 10 or more paid engagements in 30 days, or 3 plus a second signal, and a company with an open deal goes to the deal owner. When someone writes, they name the public signal, never the ad, the click or the visit.”

voices.name: Ivars Krutainis
voices.quote: “Yes, big fan. We report the list of engaged companies weekly for sales to follow up.”

title: Grow a signal list by adding signal lists from the same market
why: LinkedIn's audience size guidance fits audiences built from filters. A list built from buying signals starts smaller and grows a different way.

advises.text: An ad set needs at least 300 members to run. To drive results, LinkedIn recommends larger audiences: 50,000 members, and 300,000 for Sponsored Content.

page.adds: Those sizes fit audiences built from targeting filters. A signal list starts smaller, around 1,000 companies and 5,000 to 10,000 people. Grow it by adding signal lists from the same market, and leave fit-only companies in the cold layer. Never widen a signal list just to hit a size.
page.reason: A signal list is small because it's specific: these companies have a reason to buy now. Pad it with companies that only fit, and delivery spreads across them while the signal companies see you less.
page.mattersLess: For broad demand generation built from targeting filters, LinkedIn's sizes are a fair target.

signs.see: A signal list well under LinkedIn's suggested size
signs.do: Run it once it clears 300 members. Add signal lists from the same market to grow it.

signs.see: A signal list padded with fit-only companies to reach a size
signs.do: Move them out to the cold layer.

signs.see: A market too small to fill even one signal list
signs.do: Check the market is big enough for paid LinkedIn before you build more lists.

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “My lists start at 1,000 companies, and 10,000 is better. I get to LinkedIn's number by adding signal lists from the same market. My floor is the market: at least 10,000 decision-makers and deals worth $10,000 or more.”

title: Judge cold ads by the warm audience they build
why: A cold ad's real output is the people who engage with it, because they become your retargeting audience. Leads from cold are a bonus.

advises.text: Campaign Manager reports cold and retargeting campaigns on the same metrics, and lets you build retargeting audiences from video viewers and ad engagers.

page.adds: Measure cold in-feed on reach into your target accounts and on cost per new engager or video viewer. Build cold creative to earn that engagement, with video and document ads people can watch or read without leaving the feed.
page.reason: People rarely convert the first time they see a brand, so a cold campaign judged on leads looks like a failure and gets cut. When it goes, the retargeting audiences it was filling stop growing, and a few weeks later the warm campaigns run out of people.
page.mattersLess: Cost per lead is a fair verdict for a cold campaign built to convert on first contact, like a light content offer on a Lead Gen Form (rule 11).

signs.see: A cold campaign paused for a high cost per lead
signs.do: Count the engagers, viewers and engaged accounts it added before you write it off.

signs.see: Cold ads asking for a form fill or a demo
signs.do: Lead with something to watch or read. Keep the ask for warm (rule 11).

signs.see: 90-day engager and viewer audiences stopped growing
signs.do: Refresh the cold creative or open a new segment.

voices.name: AJ Wilcox
voices.quote: “Love this concept! One of my skills is going to play into this. I measure cold ad sets by very different standards than my warm stages. For cold, I calculate a metric called Cost Per Retargetable Member (CPRM), which measures how much it costs per member of my retargeting audience.”

voices.name: Bogdan Liutic
voices.quote: “Agree, with one catch. One of my ad sets ran on a company list built from engagement data plus LinkedIn's own engaged-companies segment, and it got 49% of its clicks from people listed at ‘Stealth AI Startup’. So strip placeholder pages before an engager audience becomes your retargeting list.”

title: No-Deal Warm Leads Finder
description: Finds companies that engage with your LinkedIn ads or website but are not customers and have no open deal, so sales knows who to call. Screens out agencies, schools and noise, and ranks the rest in tiers.

does.headline: It reads your exports.
does.context: And changes nothing in your accounts.
body: You bring: LinkedIn Companies export (last 90 days). Website visitors-by-company export from your visitor identification tool (optional, recommended). CRM companies and deals exports.
You get back: A ranked top-20 list in tiers (companies engaged on both channels first), a short 'check by hand' list, and the full list as a CSV when it is long.

title: Account Health Check

You get back: A prioritised list of at most 10 items (P1 fix now, P2 this month, P3 tidy-up), each with evidence, the fix and the expected impact, plus what could not be checked.

title: Who's Looking at Your Buying Pages
description: Shows who recently visited your high-intent pages (pricing, demo, contact, trial), at the level your visitor tool allows, ranked by seniority and checked against the CRM, with a light first step for the top few.

does.headline: It reads your exports.
does.context: And changes nothing in your accounts.
body: You bring: Website visitor export from an identification tool (last 14 days, person or company level). CRM companies and deals exports. Your website address and the buying-page URLs you care about.

body: Runs on: LinkedIn API or a Campaign Manager export. DemandSense MCP later.

steps.title: Pull the numbers
steps.text: Get spend, clicks and landing-page clicks per campaign for a date range. Stop if there are no landing-page clicks.

steps.title: Keep campaigns that spent
steps.text: Lead Gen Form campaigns go in a separate block.

steps.title: Work out the costs
steps.text: Landing-page CPC, regular CPC and the share of clicks that reach the site.

steps.title: Sort
steps.text: Best to worst. Campaigns with no site clicks go last.

steps.title: Roll up
steps.text: Blended totals for the account and a rollup by format (Thought Leader, image, video, Spotlight).

steps.title: Show the totals
steps.text: Print the totals used, so they can be matched against Campaign Manager.

title: Lowest bid that still spends the budget

does.headline: What it does.
does.context: Finds the lowest manual bid that still spends the full daily budget, because a higher bid doesn't buy a better audience.
body: Runs on: Campaign Manager daily export.
You get back: A bid recommendation per ad set.

steps.title: Export
steps.text: Export ad data by day.

steps.title: Check two days
steps.text: On Wednesday, check average daily spend for Monday and Tuesday. On Monday, check last Thursday and Friday.

steps.title: Lower the bid
steps.text: If average spend is at or above the daily budget, lower the bid.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Repeat after each bid change until the bid just barely spends the budget.

title: Cost per retargetable member

steps.title: Pick the action
steps.text: Pick the retargeting action each cold ad set feeds (for example 50% video viewers or document engagers).

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: Divide cost by the number of those actions.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Compare ad type and objective combinations and track them over time.

title: Warm-lead handoff
description: Turns engagement from LinkedIn ads, the website and the CRM into a short list of who sales should call this week.
youNeed: LinkedIn Companies export, website visitors by company, CRM exports. Or the DemandSense MCP.
youGet: An "Act now" list with a one-line handoff for each account, customers engaging, open deals reached, closed-lost to re-engage, an ad exclusion list, up to five recommendations and the full list as a CSV.

steps.title: Clean the signal
steps.text: Remove your own company, competitors, ISPs, bots, and capped or stale exports.

steps.title: Fit and rank
steps.text: Keep accounts that fit your ICP and rank them by how warm they are.

steps.title: Match to the CRM
steps.text: Customers go to their owner as expansion, open deals to the deal owner, new accounts to the SDR queue.

steps.title: Hand off
steps.text: Write a one-line handoff per account: who, what they read, which ad, who owns it.

get.context: It reads your exports and changes nothing

title: Account audit by cadence
description: Runs eight account checks on a schedule, so a LinkedIn Ads specialist knows what to fix today, this week and this month.
youNeed: Campaign Manager exports. Or the DemandSense MCP.
youGet: Daily flags plus an action list for each cadence, every item waiting for approval.

steps.title: Daily: read and flag
steps.text: Bidding and delivery, how ads engage, acquisition costs, audience saturation (frequency per person over 30 and 90 days).

steps.title: Weekly: adjust
steps.text: Bid and pacing adjustments, week-over-week trends, delivery fixes.

steps.title: Every two weeks: fatigue and pacing
steps.text: Ad fatigue (pause, scale, new tests with 2 to 3 variations per ad set) and a pacing check against the monthly target (within 5%).

steps.title: Monthly: move the budget
steps.text: Review the budget and move it between campaigns, ad sets and funnel stages.

steps.title: Approve
steps.text: Every change is a recommendation the specialist approves and applies in Campaign Manager.

title: Targeting vs who actually buys
description: Compares who each campaign paid to reach with the people on your deals, and moves budget toward the profiles that buy.
youNeed: Campaign Manager demographics export plus CRM deals. Or the DemandSense MCP.
youGet: Spend vs pipeline per buyer profile, changes per campaign and an exclusion list that's safe to apply.

steps.title: Job title audit
steps.text: Who each campaign paid to reach, graded against that campaign's own targeting.

steps.title: Read the deal side
steps.text: The buying-committee list is the base, titles on deal contacts are evidence (they're often patchy).

steps.title: Group deals by profile
steps.text: Pipeline created, win rate, deal size.

steps.title: Spend against pipeline
steps.text: Compare each profile's share of spend with its share of pipeline. Flag profiles that get too much budget, too little, or never convert.

steps.title: Recommend
steps.text: Targeting, exclusion and budget changes per campaign. Before cutting a title, check whether it sits in an account showing buying signals.

steps.title: Light check
steps.text: Is new spend leaking to off-target titles?

title: Company-level account routing
description: Shows which companies take most of the impressions, which are underserved, and which to prioritize or move into their own audience.
youNeed: LinkedIn Companies tab export. Or the DemandSense MCP.
youGet: A coverage and engagement view per campaign and a list of recommendations the advertiser decides on.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.text: Which companies get most of the impressions, which are underserved, and whether the campaign reaches the companies it meant to target.

steps.title: Engagement
steps.text: Which companies engage, which don't, and how that changes over time. Flag accounts for retargeting or sales outreach.

steps.title: Spend check
steps.text: Is the campaign spending on existing customers, closed-lost or open-deal accounts?

steps.title: Recommend
steps.text: Dynamic exclusion audiences, dedicated campaigns for some accounts, or more segmentation.

steps.title: Review before any change
steps.text: Check every recommendation against the ICP, account priorities and strategy. Nothing is excluded automatically.

title: LinkedIn fit gate + daily fit check
description: Grades a prospecting campaign by the companies it actually reached against your ICP, then says scale, run one more week, or rebuild.
youNeed: DemandSense MCP plus Apollo, CRM or a CSV.
youGet: A one-line status, fit rate, fail reasons, a verdict and an exclusion CSV to upload to LinkedIn.

steps.title: Set the gate
steps.text: Before launch, once: countries, employee range, one buyer signal (for example "runs paid ads") and exclusions (own domain, customers, open deals, competitors).

steps.title: Pull the companies
steps.text: The companies one campaign reached.

steps.title: Clean domains
steps.text: Any excluded company that was reached is a "leaked exclusion" and goes to the top.

steps.title: Apply the gate
steps.text: Check each domain in the fit source (Apollo, CRM or a CSV).

steps.title: Grade
steps.text: Fit rate and spend-weighted fit. Once 500 companies are graded: 80%+ scale, 70 to 80% one more week with tighter exclusions, under 70% rebuild.

steps.title: Daily check
steps.text: Compare with yesterday (new companies, new fails, new leaks, fit trend) and update the exclusion list.

title: Signal loop
description: Turns a list of target companies, sorted by dated public buying signals, into a Monday short list of who to write to this week and why now.
youNeed: Campaign Manager exports plus your own CSVs. The DemandSense MCP adds engagement, visits, CRM status and lead forms.
youGet: A, B and C lists with LinkedIn upload files, names to exclude, up to 5 outreach cards a week and a CRM hand-off CSV.

steps.title: Signal list check
steps.text: Split the target list into A (2+ fresh signals), B (1 signal) and C (fit only). Hold out 100 B companies with no ads all quarter.

steps.title: Placeholder page check
steps.text: Strike clicks from fake employer pages like "Stealth AI Startup".

steps.title: List dose check
steps.text: Is each list still reaching new people? About 5 views a person a month on warm lists.

steps.title: Warm account router
steps.text: Alert at 10+ paid engagements in 30 days, or 3 plus a second signal. Open deals go to their owner. Up to 5 cards a week.

steps.title: A person writes
steps.text: A person approves each card and writes from their own account. Messages name the public signal only, never the ad or the visit.

steps.title: Retrain
steps.text: Check which signals sat on won deals and retrain the lists.

title: Turn social signals into pipeline
description: Takes people engaging with relevant LinkedIn posts, adds what their companies do on your site and with your ads, and splits them into a sales list and a nurture list.
youNeed: Cornersight plus the DemandSense MCP. Or Cornersight's export plus visitor and Companies tab exports.
youGet: Two lists (sales review and nurture) with a one-line reason per company. Nothing is written to any tool.

steps.title: Pick the source
steps.text: Posts anywhere on LinkedIn (Cornersight), your company page (DemandSense), or both.

steps.title: Collect
steps.text: Collect the engagers and group them by company.

steps.title: Add signals
steps.text: Website sessions, pricing or demo page views, ad engagement level per company.

steps.title: Fit
steps.text: Keep companies that fit the ICP.

steps.title: Split
steps.text: Sales review = ICP fit + organic signal + a website visit or high ad engagement. Everyone else goes to nurture.

steps.title: CRM check
steps.text: Optional: companies already in pipeline go to the deal owner.

title: Weekly check for conversion campaigns
description: Judges every Lead Gen Form and Message ad against your goal cost per lead, pauses losers early and builds new versions from the winners.
youNeed: Campaign Manager exports (ads by day, campaign penetration and frequency, settings). Or the DemandSense MCP.
youGet: A pause list, winners to copy and campaign fixes, each with the number behind it and the number that shows it worked next week.

steps.title: Scope
steps.text: Lead gen and Message campaigns that spent in the last 7 days. Skip any without a goal cost per lead.

steps.title: Ads with no leads
steps.text: Flag pause once the ad has spent 2x the goal cost per lead.

steps.title: Ads with leads
steps.text: Flag pause when cost per lead reaches 1.5x the campaign's baseline.

steps.title: Winners
steps.text: Ads at or under goal. The top 2 become the source for new versions with the same offer.

steps.title: Check the campaign
steps.text: If every ad is expensive: delivery (spend vs daily budget, manual bid), audience size (penetration under 10% means budget too small or audience too big, 20%+ is ideal) and audience quality.

steps.title: Recommend
steps.text: One recommendation per flagged ad or campaign, each approved by the specialist.
